newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Price rises vital to avert Buglarian energy crisis.
newsitem.headline: Price rises vital to avert Buglarian energy crisis.

text.p: Bulgaria's energy sector is obliged to continue regular price rises regardless of the hardship they cause to ordinary people, energy officials say.

Under the pricing mechanism in force since last July, energy prices have been revised each month mainly according to inflation and the lev/dollar exchange rate. But rising prices of electricity are choking the economy and the overstretched budgets of ordinary people.
"With this pricing scheme...we can rely on some income and thus make future plans," Deputy Energy Minister Ivanka Dilovska said in an interview.
Since the scheme started, debt-ridden energy firms have started paying taxes and the National Electricity Company has paid six billion levs out of its 10 billion lev debt, she said.
But the impact of the scheme is delayed. "The January prices, for example, are based on the lev/dollar rate in the first 15 days of December which was 405 levs."
The lev hit new lows near 900 to the dollar on the interbank market on Thursday and its collapse will drastically increase the cost of fuel imports.

Last October the government froze heating prices when they were $15 per gigacalory. "In the stabilising programme (of the energy sector) we envisaged $20 per gigacalory while now it is only $5," Dilovska said.
She said energy price created an immediate direct inflation of four percent for other producers and 10 percent for final consumers of industrial goods.
Eventual implementation of a tough fixed exchange rate mechanism proposed by the IMF will ease matters for the ministry.
"When a currency board is implemented we will not bother with monthly revisions and will only balance the tariffs," Dilovska said.

The energy sector, which imports 86 percent of its resources, needs a greater hard currency profit, officials said. It can be won through electricity exports when the country has free capacity and through awarding concessions to existing gas pipelines transiting Russian natural gas to the Balkans.
Concessions can be offered also for big enterprises and heating plants, Dilovska said.
"But we need an energy law to be adopted (by parliament) as it would give us green light to the (electricity) company's decentralisation and privatisation," Dilovska said.
